cor-abelian-irreducibles-are-lines.title: Over an Algebraically Closed Field, Commutative Means One-Dimensional
cor-abelian-irreducibles-are-lines.title_html: Over an Algebraically Closed Field, Commutative Means One-Dimensional
cor-abelian-irreducibles-are-lines.html: Let F be algebraically closed, let A be a commutative F-algebra, and let V be an irreducible A-space. Then dim⁡V=1.

cor-column-orthogonality.title: Orthogonality of the columns
cor-column-orthogonality.html: Let G be a finite group with conjugacy classes C1,…,Ck, representatives gj∈Cj and sizes cj=|Cj|, and irreducible characters χ1,…,χk. Then for all j,l, ∑i=1kχi(gj)χi(gl)―={|G|/cj,j=l,0,j≠l.

cor-commuting-with-irreducible.title: An Operator Commuting with an Irreducible Family Is a Scalar
cor-commuting-with-irreducible.title_html: An Operator Commuting with an Irreducible Family Is a Scalar
cor-commuting-with-irreducible.html: Let F be algebraically closed, let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, and let F⊆L(V) act irreducibly. If S∈L(V) commutes with every member of F, then S=λidV for some λ∈F.

cor-complete-reducibility.title: Complete Reducibility of Group Representations
cor-complete-reducibility.html: Let G be a finite group and F a field with charF∤|G| — for instance F=C. Then every representation ρ of G on a non-zero finite-dimensional space V over F decomposes as V=V1⊕V2⊕⋯⊕Vr with each Vi a G-invariant subspace on which the subrepresentation is irreducible.

cor-dimension-count.title: Counting Dimensions in the Wedderburn Form
cor-dimension-count.title_html: Counting Dimensions in the Wedderburn Form
cor-dimension-count.html: In the situation of @thm-wedderburn, dimF⁡A=n12+⋯+nk2, and the center Z(A)={z∈A:za=az for all a∈A} has dimF⁡Z(A)=k.

cor-irreducibility-criterion.title: Irreducibility criterion
cor-irreducibility-criterion.html: Let ρ be a complex representation of a finite group G on V≠{0}, with character χ. Write V=V1⊕⋯⊕Vr with each Vi irreducible (@cor-complete-reducibility), and let χ1,…,χs be the distinct characters occurring among the χρ|Vi, with multiplicities m1,…,ms≥1. Then χ=∑i=1smiχi,mi=⟨χ,χi⟩,⟨χ,χ⟩=∑i=1smi2. In particular ⟨χ,χ⟩=1 if and only if ρ is irreducible, and two complex representations of G with the same character are equivalent.

cor-irreducible-set-spans.title: An Irreducible Multiplicative Set Spans the Whole Algebra
cor-irreducible-set-spans.title_html: An Irreducible Multiplicative Set Spans the Whole Algebra
cor-irreducible-set-spans.html: Let F be algebraically closed, V a vector space over F with 1≤dim⁡V<∞, and let S⊆End(V) be a set with idV∈S that is closed under composition. If the only subspaces U⊆V with s(U)⊆U for all s∈S are {0} and V, then span(S)=End(V).

cor-matrix-homomorphism-injective.title: Homomorphisms out of a Matrix Algebra Are Injective
cor-matrix-homomorphism-injective.title_html: Homomorphisms out of a Matrix Algebra Are Injective
cor-matrix-homomorphism-injective.html: Let F be a field, n≥1, and let φ:Mn(F)→B be an algebra homomorphism into any F-algebra B≠{0}. Then φ is injective.

cor-schur-common-eigenvector.title: Commuting Operators Have a Common Eigenvector
cor-schur-common-eigenvector.title_html: Commuting Operators Have a Common Eigenvector
cor-schur-common-eigenvector.html: Let F be algebraically closed, let V≠{0} be finite-dimensional over F, and let F⊆L(V) be a family whose members commute with one another. Then there is v≠0 that is an eigenvector of every T∈F.

cor-sum-of-squares.title: The sum of the squares of the degrees
cor-sum-of-squares.title_html: The sum of the squares of the degrees
cor-sum-of-squares.html: Let G be a finite group and let ρ1,…,ρk on V1,…,Vk be a complete list of pairwise inequivalent irreducible complex representations of G, one for each of the k conjugacy classes (@thm-characters-span-class-functions). Then each ρi occurs in the regular representation with multiplicity exactly dim⁡Vi, and |G|=∑i=1k(dim⁡Vi)2.

cor-weyr-commutant-revisited.title: The Commutant of a Single Operator
cor-weyr-commutant-revisited.title_html: The Commutant of a Single Operator
cor-weyr-commutant-revisited.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, let T∈L(V), and let A=F[T]⊆End(V) be the algebra of all polynomials in T. Then A′={S∈L(V):ST=TS}. Consequently the following two earlier results are computations of A′.

  1. If F=C and the matrix of T in some basis is A1⊕⋯⊕Ar with the Ap of pairwise disjoint spectra, then in that same basis every member of A′ has a block diagonal matrix for the partition into those block sizes (@cor-commutant-block-diagonal).
  2. If the matrix of T in some basis is a basic Weyr matrix of Weyr structure (w1,…,ws), then in that same basis every member of A′ has a block upper triangular matrix for the partition w1+⋯+ws (@prp-weyr-commutant).

If moreover T is diagonalizable with distinct eigenvalues λ1,…,λk and di=dim⁡Eλi(T), then A acts semisimply, dim⁡A=k, dim⁡A′=∑i=1kdi2, and A″=A.

def-algebra-homomorphism.title: Algebra Homomorphism, Kernel and Image
def-algebra-homomorphism.html: Let A and B be algebras over F. An algebra homomorphism φ:A→B is an F-linear map with φ(xy)=φ(x)φ(y)for all x,y∈A,φ(1A)=1B, as in @def-algebra-over-field. Its kernel is kerφ={x∈A:φ(x)=0} and its image is imφ={φ(x):x∈A}, the kernel and image of φ as a linear map.

def-algebra-isomorphism.title: Isomorphic Algebras
def-algebra-isomorphism.html: An algebra isomorphism is a bijective algebra homomorphism. Algebras A and B are isomorphic, written A≅B, if there is an algebra isomorphism A→B.

def-algebra-radical.title: Radical of an Algebra
def-algebra-radical.html: Let A be an F-algebra. Its radical is radA:=⋂V{a∈A:aV={0}}, where V runs over all irreducible A-spaces and aV={av:v∈V}.

def-character.title: Character
def-character.html: Let ρ be a representation of a finite group G on a finite-dimensional complex vector space V. The character of ρ is the function χρ:G→C,χρ(g):=trρ(g). Its degree is χρ(1)=dim⁡V. A character is irreducible if ρ is irreducible (@def-irreducible-representation).

def-character-inner-product.title: The inner product of class functions
def-character-inner-product.title_html: The inner product of class functions
def-character-inner-product.html: For functions f,f′:G→C on a finite group G, set ⟨f,f′⟩:=1|G|∑g∈Gf(g)f′(g)―.

def-character-matrix.title: Character matrix
def-character-matrix.html: Let G be a finite abelian group of order n. Fix an ordering g0,…,gn−1 of G and an ordering χ0,…,χn−1 of G^, which has n elements too (@prp-dual-group-order). The character matrix of G for those orderings is U∈Mn(C) with (U)mj:=χj(gm)n(0≤m,j≤n−1). Its j-th column lists the values of χj, scaled by n−1/2.

def-class-function.title: Class function
def-class-function.html: Let G be a finite group. A function f:G→C is a class function if f(xgx−1)=f(g) for all g,x∈G; equivalently, if f is constant on each conjugacy class. The set of class functions is written Cl(G).

def-commutant.title: Commutant and Center
def-commutant.html: Let A be an algebra over F and let S⊆A be any subset. The commutant of S in A is S′:={a∈A:as=sa for every s∈S}. The center of A is Z(A):=A′, the set of elements commuting with every element of A. We write S″ for (S′)′.

def-conjugacy-class.title: Conjugate elements, conjugacy class
def-conjugacy-class.html: Let G be a group. Elements g,h∈G are conjugate if h=xgx−1 for some x∈G. The conjugacy class of g is C(g):={xgx−1:x∈G}.

def-cyclic-group.title: Cyclic group
def-cyclic-group.html: A group G is cyclic if G=⟨g⟩ for some g∈G; such a g is called a generator of G. A cyclic group is abelian, since gkgl=gk+l=glgk.

def-direct-product-of-groups.title: Direct product of groups
def-direct-product-of-groups.html: Let G and H be groups. Their direct product G×H is the set of ordered pairs (g,h) with the componentwise operation (g,h)(g′,h′):=(gg′,hh′). It is a group, with identity (eG,eH) and (g,h)−1=(g−1,h−1); the three axioms are checked one component at a time. It is abelian when G and H are, and |G×H|=|G||H|.

def-dual-group.title: Dual group
def-dual-group.html: Let G be a finite abelian group. The dual group of G is G^:={χ:G→C×:χ is a group homomorphism}, with the pointwise operation (χψ)(g):=χ(g)ψ(g). Its elements are the characters of G.

def-equivalent-representations.title: Equivalence of representations
def-equivalent-representations.html: Let ρ and ρ′ be representations of G on V and V′, over the same field. A linear map S:V→V′ intertwines ρ and ρ′ if Sρ(g)=ρ′(g)Sfor every g∈G. The representations are equivalent, written ρ≅ρ′, if some intertwining S is an isomorphism; equivalently, if ρ′(g)=Sρ(g)S−1 for all g.

def-fourier-transform-on-a-group.title: Fourier transform on a finite abelian group
def-fourier-transform-on-a-group.title_html: Fourier transform on a finite abelian group
def-fourier-transform-on-a-group.html: Let G be a finite abelian group of order n and let f:G→C. The Fourier transform of f is the function f^:G^→C given by f^(χ):=∑g∈Gf(g)χ(g).

def-generated-subalgebra.title: The Subalgebra Generated by a Set
def-generated-subalgebra.title_html: The Subalgebra Generated by a Set
def-generated-subalgebra.html: Let A be an algebra over F and S⊆A. The subalgebra generated by S, written F⟨S⟩, is the intersection of all subalgebras of A containing S.

def-group-algebra.title: Group Algebra
def-group-algebra.html: Let G be a finite group with identity e, and let F be a field. The group algebra F[G] is the free vector space F(G) on the set G (@def-free-vector-space), with basis {δg:g∈G}, equipped with the unique bilinear multiplication satisfying δgδh=δghfor all g,h∈G. We write g for δg and 1 for δe, so that a general element is a formal sum ∑g∈Gagg with all ag∈F, two such sums are equal exactly when all their coefficients agree, and (∑gagg)(∑hbhh)=∑k∈G(∑g∈Gagbg−1k)k.

def-intertwining-map.title: A-Map, and Isomorphism of A-spaces
def-intertwining-map.title_html: A-Map, and Isomorphism of A-spaces
def-intertwining-map.html: Let A be an F-algebra and let V and W be A-spaces. A linear map φ:V→W is an A-map if φ(av)=aφ(v)for every a∈A and every v∈V. We write EndA(V) for the set of A-maps from V to itself. A bijective A-map is an isomorphism of A-spaces, and V and W are isomorphic if one exists.

def-irreducible-representation.title: Irreducible representation
def-irreducible-representation.html: A representation ρ of G on V is irreducible if V≠{0} and the only G-invariant subspaces of V are {0} and V. A representation with V≠{0} that is not irreducible is reducible.

def-left-ideal.title: Left and Right Ideals
def-left-ideal.html:
Let A be an algebra over F and let I⊆A be a subspace. Then I is

  1. a left ideal of A if ax∈I for every a∈A and every x∈I;
  2. a right ideal of A if xa∈I for every a∈A and every x∈I.

A two-sided ideal is a subspace that is both, which is @def-two-sided-ideal. When A is commutative the three notions coincide, and we say ideal.

def-product-of-algebras.title: Product of algebras
def-product-of-algebras.html: Let A1,…,Ak be F-algebras. Their product A1×⋯×Ak is the product vector space (@def-product-of-spaces) with multiplication defined slot by slot, (x1,…,xk)(y1,…,yk)=(x1y1,…,xkyk), and identity (1A1,…,1Ak).

def-quotient-algebra.title: Quotient Algebra
def-quotient-algebra.html: Let A be an algebra over F and I a two-sided ideal of A. The quotient algebra A/I is the quotient vector space A/I with the multiplication (x+I)(y+I)=xy+I of @lem-quotient-algebra, and π:A→A/I, π(x)=x+I, is the quotient homomorphism.

def-representation.title: Representation of a group
def-representation.html: Let G be a group, F a field and V a finite-dimensional vector space over F. A representation of G on V over F is a group homomorphism ρ:G→GL(V), that is, a map assigning to each g∈G an invertible operator ρ(g) on V such that ρ(gh)=ρ(g)ρ(h) for all g,h∈G. The space V is the representation space, and dim⁡V is the degree of ρ. The representation is faithful if ρ is injective. When V=Fn we speak of a matrix representation and write ρ(g)∈GLn(F).

def-representation-of-an-algebra.title: Representation of an Algebra, and Invariant Subspaces
def-representation-of-an-algebra.title_html: Representation of an Algebra, and Invariant Subspaces
def-representation-of-an-algebra.html: Let A be an F-algebra. A representation of A on a finite-dimensional vector space V over F is an algebra homomorphism ρ:A→L(V), so that ρ is linear, ρ(ab)=ρ(a)ρ(b), and ρ(1A)=idV. We then call V an A-space and abbreviate ρ(a)(v) to av. A subspace U⊆V is A-invariant if au∈U for every a∈A and every u∈U.

def-semisimple-algebra.title: Semisimple Action, Semisimple Algebra
def-semisimple-algebra.html: Let A be an F-algebra and V an A-space. We say A acts semisimply on V if every A-invariant subspace U⊆V has an A-invariant complement: a subspace W⊆V with V=U⊕WandW is A-invariant. The algebra A is semisimple if it acts semisimply on itself in the regular representation — that is, if every left ideal of A has a complementary left ideal.

def-simple-algebra.title: Simple Algebra
def-simple-algebra.html: An F-algebra A is simple if A≠{0} and the only two-sided ideals (@def-two-sided-ideal) of A are {0} and A itself.

def-simple-module.title: Irreducible, or Simple, A-space
def-simple-module.title_html: Irreducible, or Simple, A-space
def-simple-module.html: An A-space V is irreducible — equivalently, simple — if V≠{0} and the only A-invariant subspaces of V are {0} and V.

def-subalgebra.title: Subalgebra
def-subalgebra.html:
Let A be an algebra over F. A subset B⊆A is a subalgebra of A if

  1. B is a subspace of A;
  2. xy∈B for all x,y∈B;
  3. 1A∈B.

def-subrepresentation.title: Subrepresentation
def-subrepresentation.html: Let ρ be a representation of G on V. A subspace U⊆V is G-invariant if ρ(g)u∈U for every g∈G and every u∈U. In that case the restrictions ρ(g)|U define a representation ρ|U of G on U, the subrepresentation of ρ on U.

exm-first-ideals.html:

  2. In F[x]: the sets ⟨p⟩ of @def-ideal-polynomials.
  3. In Mn(F): the column ideal Cj of matrices whose columns other than the j-th are zero.
  4. In Mn(F): the set RU={X:col(X)⊆U} for a subspace U⊆Fn.
  5. In any algebra A: the kernel of an algebra homomorphism φ:A→B.

  4. The quaternions H inside M2(C), as an algebra over R.
  5. The strictly upper triangular matrices inside Mn(F).
  6. The matrices of trace 0 inside M2(F).

  4. {cidV+N:c∈F, N2=0} inside L(V), for dim⁡V=3.

exr-associative-algebras-b2.title: B2: A commutant
exr-associative-algebras-b2.html: Let D=diag(1,1,2)∈M3(Q). Compute {D}′ and its dimension, and compare it with dim⁡Q[D]. Hence show that {D}′≠Q[D].

exr-associative-algebras-b3.title: B3: Cayley for the quaternions
exr-associative-algebras-b3.html: Let H be the quaternions with ordered basis B=(1,i,j,k) over R, where 1 denotes I2. Compute the matrices of Li and Lj in B, and verify that they satisfy Li2=−I4 and LiLj=Lk.

exr-associative-algebras-c1.title: C1: The center of a group algebra
exr-associative-algebras-c1.title_html: C1: The center of a group algebra
exr-associative-algebras-c1.html:
Let G be a finite group and F a field. For g∈G, the conjugacy class of g is Kg={hgh−1:h∈G}, and the class sum is zg=∑k∈Kgk∈F[G].

  1. Prove that x=∑gagg lies in Z(F[G]) if and only if ahgh−1=ag for all g,h∈G.
  2. Deduce that the distinct class sums form a basis of Z(F[G]), so that dim⁡Z(F[G]) is the number of conjugacy classes of G.
  3. Compute dim⁡Z(F[S3]).

Hint for (a): by bilinearity it is enough to test commutation against the basis elements h∈G.

exr-associative-algebras-c2.title: C2: Generated by two matrix units
exr-associative-algebras-c2.title_html: C2: Generated by two matrix units
exr-associative-algebras-c2.html:
Work in M2(F).

  1. Compute F⟨{E12}⟩ and its dimension.
  2. Compute F⟨{E12,E21}⟩ and its dimension.
  3. Deduce that adding one generator can change the commutant from an algebra of dimension 2 to the scalars, and compute both commutants.

exr-associative-algebras-c3.title: C3: Is the group algebra ever a field?
exr-associative-algebras-c3.title_html: C3: Is the group algebra ever a field?
exr-associative-algebras-c3.html:
Let G be a finite group with |G|≥2 and let F be any field.

  1. Pick g≠e in G of order m≥2, meaning gm=e and gi≠e for 1≤i<m. (Such an m exists: the powers g,g2,… cannot all be distinct in a finite group, and canceling gives gi=e for some i≥1.) Show that x=1−g and y=1+g+⋯+gm−1 satisfy xy=0 with x≠0 and y≠0.
  2. Deduce that F[G] is never a field, and never isomorphic to a subalgebra of a field.
  3. Is F[G] ever commutative for |G|≥2? Give an example or a proof that it is not.

exr-characters-a1.title: A1
exr-characters-a1.html:
1. Define the character of a representation, and state why it does not depend on a choice of basis.
  2. State the orthogonality relation for irreducible complex characters.
  3. Determine whether the following is true: “if χ is a character of G then χ(gh)=χ(g)χ(h).” Justify your answer.
  4. A group of order 12 has exactly four conjugacy classes. Determine the degrees of its irreducible complex representations.
  5. Explain why the number of irreducible complex representations of an abelian group G is |G|.

exr-characters-b1.title: B1: A character computed and decomposed
exr-characters-b1.title_html: B1: A character computed and decomposed
exr-characters-b1.html:
Let Pτ be the permutation matrix of τ∈S3, so that Pτei=eτ(i) (@def-permutation-matrix), and let π be the representation of S3 on L(C3) given by π(τ)(f)=PτfPτ−1.

  1. Compute the character of π on the three conjugacy classes.
  2. Decompose π into irreducibles.

exr-characters-b2.title: B2: Which of these are characters?
exr-characters-b2.title_html: B2: Which of these are characters?
exr-characters-b2.html:
Let G=S3, with classes ordered id, (1 2), (1 2 3) of sizes 1,3,2. Determine which of the following class functions are characters of complex representations of S3. Justify your answer.

  1. (4,0,1);
  2. (3,1,0);
  3. (2,2,−1);
  4. (1,1,−1).

exr-characters-b3.title: B3: Degree-one characters of a cyclic group
exr-characters-b3.title_html: B3: Degree-one characters of a cyclic group
exr-characters-b3.html:
Let G=Z/6Z.

  1. Write down the character table.
  2. Verify ⟨χ1,χ4⟩=0 and ⟨χ2,χ2⟩=1 by direct computation.

exr-characters-c1.title: C1: Counting fixed points
exr-characters-c1.html:
Let G be a finite group acting on {1,…,n} through a homomorphism φ:G→Sn, and let ρ(g)=Pφ(g) be the corresponding permutation representation on Cn, where Pσ is the permutation matrix of @def-permutation-matrix (so PσPτ=Pστ by @lem-permutation-matrices (a)).

  1. Prove that ⟨χρ,χtriv⟩ equals the average number of fixed points of the permutations φ(g), and also equals dim⁡(Cn)G.
  2. Deduce that for every n≥1, the average number of fixed points of a permutation in Sn is exactly 1.
  3. For G=S3 with φ=id, verify (a) numerically.

exr-characters-c2.title: C2: Degree-one characters form a group
exr-characters-c2.title_html: C2: Degree-one characters form a group
exr-characters-c2.html:
Let G be a finite group and let X(G) be the set of characters of degree 1 of complex representations of G. (For abelian G this group is the subject of Section 09.)

  1. Prove that the pointwise product of two degree-one characters is a degree-one character, and that X(G) is a group under this product.
  2. Prove that |X(G)|≤k, the number of conjugacy classes, with equality if and only if G is abelian. Hint: use @cor-sum-of-squares in one direction and @cor-abelian-irreducibles-are-lines in the other.

exr-characters-c3.title: C3: The second orthogonality relation
exr-characters-c3.html:
Let G be a finite group with irreducible complex characters χ1,…,χk.

  1. Prove that ∑i=1k|χi(g)|2=|G|/|C(g)| for every g∈G.
  2. Deduce that ∑i|χi(g)|2=1 if and only if the class of g is all of G, and that this happens only for the trivial group. Hint: C(1)={1} always.
  3. For G=S3 compute ∑i|χi(g)|2 at each of the three classes and check (a).

exr-double-commutant-a1.title: A1
exr-double-commutant-a1.html:
1. State Burnside’s theorem, with every hypothesis.
  2. Give the field hypothesis of @thm-double-commutant, and say why it differs from the one in (a).
  3. True or false, with a reason: if A⊆End(V) is a subalgebra containing idV, then A‴=A′.
  4. Explain in one sentence why {0} and V being the only A-invariant subspaces does not by itself imply Av=V for v≠0.

exr-double-commutant-b1.title: B1: Determine which are irreducible
exr-double-commutant-b1.html:
For each subalgebra of M2(C), determine whether it acts irreducibly on C2, and hence whether it equals M2(C). Justify your answer.

  1. The algebra generated by (0100).
  2. The algebra generated by (0110) and (100i).
  3. The algebra of all matrices (ab0a).

exr-double-commutant-b2.title: B2: A commutant and a double commutant
exr-double-commutant-b2.title_html: B2: A commutant and a double commutant
exr-double-commutant-b2.html:
Let A=diag(1,1,2)∈M3(R) and let A=R[A]⊆M3(R).

  1. Compute dim⁡A.
  2. Describe A′ explicitly and compute dim⁡A′.
  3. Compute A″, and check the answer against @thm-double-commutant.

exr-double-commutant-b3.title: B3: One theorem, once
exr-double-commutant-b3.html: Let F be algebraically closed, let V be finite-dimensional over F with dim⁡V≥2, and let A⊆End(V) be a commutative subalgebra containing idV. Prove that A does not act irreducibly on V.

exr-double-commutant-c1.title: C1: The rank-one step needs its hypothesis
exr-double-commutant-c1.title_html: C1: The rank-one step needs its hypothesis
exr-double-commutant-c1.html:
In Step 2 of the proof of @thm-burnside, the operator ab was restricted to W=ima and an eigenvalue was extracted.

  1. Prove that ab(W)⊆W, and give an example of a,b∈M2(F) with ba(ima)⊈ima, so that the order of the product matters.
  2. Take F=R, A={xI2+yQ} with Q=(0−110). Compute the minimal rank r of a non-zero member of A and confirm that the conclusion r=1 fails.
  3. Which sentence of Step 2 fails for this A? Say exactly where the hypothesis on F was used.

exr-double-commutant-c2.title: C2: Commutants under a change of basis
exr-double-commutant-c2.title_html: C2: Commutants under a change of basis
exr-double-commutant-c2.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional over F, let A⊆End(V) be a subalgebra containing idV, and let g∈End(V) be invertible. Put gAg−1={gag−1:a∈A}.

  1. Prove that gAg−1 is a subalgebra containing idV and that (gAg−1)′=gA′g−1.
  2. Deduce that if A″=A then (gAg−1)″=gAg−1.
  3. Hence show that the conclusion of @thm-double-commutant is a property of the algebra up to similarity, and use this to give, for each n≥2, a subalgebra of Mn(F) with A″≠A.

exr-double-commutant-c3.title: C3: Is this look-alike a theorem?
exr-double-commutant-c3.title_html: C3: Is this look-alike a theorem?
exr-double-commutant-c3.html:
Let V be finite-dimensional over an algebraically closed F and let A⊆End(V) be a subalgebra with idV∈A.

  1. Prove: if V is irreducible as an A-space then A′={λidV}.
  2. Is the converse true? That is, does A′={λidV} force V to be irreducible? Justify your answer.

Hint for (b): consider the upper triangular matrices in M2(F).

exr-group-representations-a1.title: A1
exr-group-representations-a1.html:
1. State the definition of a representation of a group G on a vector space V, and say which two properties of ρ come for free.
  2. State Maschke’s theorem with all of its hypotheses.
  3. Determine whether the following is true: “every representation of degree 1 is irreducible.” Justify your answer.
  4. Give an example of a reducible representation of S3 over C, and name an invariant subspace.
  5. Explain why ρ:Z/2Z→GL1(Q), ρ([k])=2k, is not a representation.

exr-group-representations-b1.title: B1: Which of these are representations?
exr-group-representations-b1.title_html: B1: Which of these are representations?
exr-group-representations-b1.html:
Determine which of the following are representations. Justify your answer in each case.

  1. G=Z/6Z, F=C, ρ([k])=(ωk00ω−k) with ω=eπi/3.
  2. G=S3, F=R, ρ(σ)=sgn(σ)Pσ, where Pσ is the permutation matrix with Pσei=eσ(i) (@def-permutation-matrix).
  3. G=S3, F=R, ρ(σ)=Pσ⊤ with Pσ as in (b).
  4. G=Z/4Z, F=R, ρ([k])=(100k+1).

exr-group-representations-b2.title: B2: Averaging an inner product
exr-group-representations-b2.html: Let G be a finite group and ρ a representation of G on a complex space V carrying an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ (@def-inner-product). Define ⟨u,v⟩G:=1|G|∑g∈G⟨ρ(g)u,ρ(g)v⟩. Prove that ⟨⋅,⋅⟩G is an inner product on V and that every ρ(g) is an isometry for it. Hence give a second proof of @thm-maschke over C.

exr-group-representations-b3.title: B3: Decomposing a permutation representation
exr-group-representations-b3.html: Number the coordinates of C3 as 0,1,2, as in Chapter 11 §09, and let G=Z/3Z act by ρ([k])=Sk, where S is the cyclic shift, Sx=(x1,x2,x0). Check that ρ is a representation, decompose C3 into one-dimensional invariant subspaces, and identify each with one of the χk of @exm-cyclic-irreducibles.

exr-group-representations-c1.title: C1: One-dimensional representations and the commutator
exr-group-representations-c1.title_html: C1: One-dimensional representations and the commutator
exr-group-representations-c1.html:
Let G be a finite group and F a field.

  1. Prove that every representation of degree 1 satisfies ρ(ghg−1h−1)=1 for all g,h∈G.
  2. Deduce that the only degree-1 complex representation of G=S3 other than the trivial one is the sign representation. Hint: write the 3-cycle (1 2 3) in the form ghg−1h−1 with g and h transpositions.

exr-group-representations-c2.title: C2: Maschke over a field of the right characteristic
exr-group-representations-c2.title_html: C2: Maschke over a field of the right characteristic
exr-group-representations-c2.html:
Let G=Z/2Z and V=F2, with ρ([1])=(0110).

  1. For F=Q, find two G-invariant lines whose direct sum is V.
  2. For F=F2, prove that V has exactly one non-trivial G-invariant subspace, and conclude that @thm-maschke fails here. Which hypothesis is violated?
  3. For F=F3, decompose V into irreducible subrepresentations.

exr-group-representations-c3.title: C3: The contragredient representation
exr-group-representations-c3.html:
Let G be a finite group and ρ a representation of G on V over F. For g∈G define τ(g):=(ρ(g)−1)′∈L(V∗), where T′ denotes the dual map (@def-dual-map).

  1. Prove that τ is a representation of G on V∗, the contragredient of ρ.
  2. Prove that if U⊆V is G-invariant for ρ, then its annihilator U0⊆V∗ (@def-annihilator) is G-invariant for τ.
  3. Hence deduce that if τ is irreducible, so is ρ.

exr-ideals-and-quotients-a1.title: A1
exr-ideals-and-quotients-a1.html:
1. Define left ideal, right ideal and two-sided ideal, and say which of the three is needed to form a quotient algebra.
  2. State the product rule for matrix units, and say which step of the proof of @thm-matrix-algebra-is-simple uses that F is a field.
  3. True or false, with a reason: a two-sided ideal of an algebra A is a subalgebra of A.
  4. Give a left ideal of M3(F) of dimension 6, and say which subspace of row vectors it corresponds to.

exr-ideals-and-quotients-b1.title: B1: Determine which are ideals
exr-ideals-and-quotients-b1.html:
Determine, for each of the following subspaces, whether it is a left ideal, a right ideal, a two-sided ideal, or none. Justify your answer.

  1. {X∈M2(F):x11+x22=0}.
  2. {X∈M2(F):row 2 of X is 0}.
  3. {X∈M3(F):Xe1=0}.
  4. {p∈F[x]:p(0)=0} inside F[x].

exr-ideals-and-quotients-b2.title: B2: A quotient computed
exr-ideals-and-quotients-b2.html:
Let A=F[x]/⟨x2⟩.

  1. Write down a basis of A and its multiplication table.
  2. Show that I=span(x+⟨x2⟩) is a two-sided ideal of A and identify A/I.
  3. Show that A is not isomorphic to F×F.

exr-ideals-and-quotients-b3.title: B3: An ideal generated
exr-ideals-and-quotients-b3.html: Inside M3(F), let I=⟨E23⟩ be the two-sided ideal generated by E23 in the sense of @def-two-sided-ideal. Compute I, and do the same for the left ideal generated by E23, that is, span{AE23:A∈M3(F)}.

exr-ideals-and-quotients-c1.title: C1: All the ideals of the upper triangular algebra
exr-ideals-and-quotients-c1.title_html: C1: All the ideals of the upper triangular algebra
exr-ideals-and-quotients-c1.html:
Let T2 be the upper triangular matrices in M2(F), with basis (E11,E12,E22).

  1. Prove that J1=span(E11,E12) and J2=span(E12,E22) are two-sided ideals.
  2. Prove that {0}, span(E12), J1, J2 and T2 are the only two-sided ideals of T2.
  3. Identify T2/J1 and T2/J2.

Hint for (b): if an ideal contains an element with a≠0, multiply it by E11 on both sides.

exr-ideals-and-quotients-c2.title: C2: Simplicity over a small field, and a failure
exr-ideals-and-quotients-c2.title_html: C2: Simplicity over a small field, and a failure
exr-ideals-and-quotients-c2.html:
1. Verify @thm-matrix-algebra-is-simple by hand for M2(F2), starting from the ideal generated by E12+E21.
  2. Let A=F×F. Show that A has exactly four two-sided ideals, and conclude that a commutative algebra of dimension 2 can fail to be simple.
  3. Deduce that M2(F) and F4=F×F×F×F are not isomorphic as F-algebras, although they have the same dimension.

exr-ideals-and-quotients-c3.title: C3: Left ideals and null spaces
exr-ideals-and-quotients-c3.title_html: C3: Left ideals and null spaces
exr-ideals-and-quotients-c3.html:
Let F be a field and n≥1.

  1. For a subspace U⊆Fn, prove that NU={X∈Mn(F):Xu=0 for every u∈U} is a left ideal of Mn(F).
  2. Prove that dim⁡NU=n(n−dim⁡U).
  3. Prove that U↦NU is an inclusion-reversing bijection from subspaces of Fn onto left ideals of Mn(F), and describe NU in the language of @prp-left-ideals-of-matrix-algebra.

Hint for (b): a matrix kills every vector of U exactly when each of its rows annihilates U.

exr-schurs-lemma-a1.title: A1
exr-schurs-lemma-a1.html:
1. State both parts of Schur’s lemma and say precisely which one needs F to be algebraically closed, and what that hypothesis is used for.
  2. True or false: if V and W are irreducible A-spaces with dim⁡V≠dim⁡W, then the only A-map V→W is 0. Justify your answer.
  3. Explain why, for an irreducible A-space V, no element of EndA(V) can be non-zero and non-invertible.
  4. Give EndA(R2) for the rotation representation of @exm-rotation-commutant-is-complex, and say which part of Schur’s lemma it illustrates and which it refutes.

exr-schurs-lemma-b1.title: B1: An irreducibility test
exr-schurs-lemma-b1.html:
Let D=diag(i,−i)∈M2(C), which satisfies D4=I2, and let A=C[D] be the algebra of polynomials in D.

  1. Compute EndA(C2).
  2. Deduce from @thm-schurs-lemma (b) that C2 is not an irreducible A-space, and confirm this by exhibiting a proper non-zero invariant subspace.

exr-schurs-lemma-b2.title: B2: The quarter turn, over two fields
exr-schurs-lemma-b2.title_html: B2: The quarter turn, over two fields
exr-schurs-lemma-b2.html:
Let Q=(0−110), the rotation by a quarter turn, and let AF=F[Q] for F=R and for F=C.

  1. Show that R2 is an irreducible AR-space and that EndAR(R2)≅C.
  2. Show that C2 is not an irreducible AC-space, and find two invariant lines.
  3. Explain why (a) and (b) together are consistent with Schur’s lemma.

exr-schurs-lemma-b3.title: B3: A common eigenvector
exr-schurs-lemma-b3.html:
Let A=(2102),B=(3503)∈M2(C).

  1. Verify that AB=BA.
  2. Find a common eigenvector, and check that it spans the unique minimal non-zero invariant subspace, as in the proof of @cor-schur-common-eigenvector.

exr-schurs-lemma-c1.title: C1: A commutant that is a field
exr-schurs-lemma-c1.title_html: C1: A commutant that is a field
exr-schurs-lemma-c1.html:
Let A=(0210)∈M2(Q), the companion matrix of x2−2, and let A=Q[A].

  1. Prove that Q2 is an irreducible A-space.
  2. Compute EndA(Q2) and prove that it is a field in which 2 has a square root.
  3. Explain why this does not contradict @thm-schurs-lemma.

exr-schurs-lemma-c2.title: C2: Scalar commutant without irreducibility
exr-schurs-lemma-c2.html:
Let F be algebraically closed — say F=C, so that @cor-commuting-with-irreducible really applies — and let A⊆M2(F) be the algebra of upper triangular matrices.

  1. Compute the set of X∈M2(F) commuting with every element of A. (The computation uses nothing about F.)
  2. Deduce that the converse of @cor-commuting-with-irreducible fails: a family with commutant the scalars need not act irreducibly.

exr-simple-and-semisimple-a1.title: A1
exr-simple-and-semisimple-a1.html:
1. State what it means for an algebra to be simple and what it means for an A-space to be irreducible, and give one object that is the first but whose regular representation is not the second.
  2. True or false: if A acts semisimply on V, then every A-invariant subspace of V is irreducible. Justify your answer.
  3. Where exactly does the proof of @prp-semisimple-algebra-all-reps-semisimple use the requirement ρ(1A)=idV built into @def-representation-of-an-algebra? And why is the step a=a1A in the proof of @prp-semisimple-has-zero-radical not an instance of that requirement?
  4. Name radA for the algebra A of upper triangular 2×2 matrices, and say which two results identify it.

exr-simple-and-semisimple-b1.title: B1: Which actions split?
exr-simple-and-semisimple-b1.html:
Determine which of the following subalgebras of M2(F), acting on V=F2, act semisimply. Justify your answer in each case, and when the action is semisimple exhibit V as a direct sum of irreducibles.

  1. the scalar matrices {cI2:c∈F};
  2. the diagonal matrices;
  3. F[N]={aI2+bN:a,b∈F}, where N=J2(0);
  4. M2(F) itself.

exr-simple-and-semisimple-b2.title: B2: A two-dimensional algebra
exr-simple-and-semisimple-b2.html:
Let N=J2(0)∈M2(F) and A={aI2+bN:a,b∈F}.

  1. Prove that A is a commutative subalgebra of M2(F) of dimension 2.
  2. Prove that FN is a two-sided ideal of A and compute radA.
  3. Is A a semisimple algebra? Justify your answer.

exr-simple-and-semisimple-b3.title: B3: Semisimple operators
exr-simple-and-semisimple-b3.html:
For each of the following, decide whether F[T] acts semisimply on V, using @thm-semisimple-operator-iff-semisimple-action.

  1. F=R, V=R2, T the rotation matrix (0−110);
  2. F=Q, V=Q3, T=diag(1,1,2);
  3. F=Q, V=Q3, T=J3(0);
  4. F=R, V=R4, T=C((x2+1)2).

exr-simple-and-semisimple-c1.title: C1: The diagonal algebra
exr-simple-and-semisimple-c1.html:
Let A⊆Mn(F) be the algebra of all diagonal matrices, acting on V=Fn.

  1. Prove that every A-invariant subspace of V is the span of a subset of {e1,…,en}. Hint: consider Eiiv.
  2. Deduce that A acts semisimply on V and identify the irreducible A-subspaces.

exr-simple-and-semisimple-c2.title: C2: The radical is never everything
exr-simple-and-semisimple-c2.title_html: C2: The radical is never everything
exr-simple-and-semisimple-c2.html:
Let A≠{0} be a finite-dimensional F-algebra.

  1. Prove that A has at least one irreducible A-space. Hint: among the non-zero left ideals, take one of smallest dimension.
  2. Prove that every irreducible A-space has dimension at most dim⁡A.
  3. Deduce that 1A∉radA, so radA≠A.

exr-summary-and-transfer-a1.title: A1
exr-summary-and-transfer-a1.html:
1. Name the four moves of this chapter and, for each, one theorem in which it was used.
  2. State the field hypothesis needed by each of @thm-schurs-lemma (second half), @thm-burnside, @thm-wedderburn and @thm-maschke.
  3. Determine whether the following are true, with a reason. (i) Every finite-dimensional complex algebra is a product of matrix algebras. (ii) Every complex representation of a finite group decomposes into irreducibles. (iii) Every representation of a finite group over every field decomposes into irreducibles. (iv) The book proves that two non-isomorphic groups can share a character table.
  4. Why is |G|=∑i(dim⁡Vi)2 useful before any matrix has been written down?

exr-summary-and-transfer-b1.title: B1: Two group algebras of order six
exr-summary-and-transfer-b1.title_html: B1: Two group algebras of order six
exr-summary-and-transfer-b1.html:
1. Write down the Wedderburn decomposition of C[Z/6Z], with a reason for each factor.
  2. The group S3 has three conjugacy classes. Use @cor-sum-of-squares to find the dimensions of its irreducible complex representations, and write down the Wedderburn decomposition of C[S3].
  3. Check both answers against dim⁡C[G]=|G|.

exr-summary-and-transfer-b2.title: B2: What the sum of squares allows at order eight
exr-summary-and-transfer-b2.title_html: B2: What the sum of squares allows at order eight
exr-summary-and-transfer-b2.html:
Let G be a group of order 8.

  1. List all the possible multisets of dimensions of the irreducible complex representations of G. Remember that the trivial representation is always present.
  2. Say which of your lists corresponds to an abelian G, and why.
  3. Deduce how many conjugacy classes a non-abelian group of order 8 has.

exr-summary-and-transfer-c1.title: C1: The circulants as a semisimple algebra
exr-summary-and-transfer-c1.title_html: C1: The circulants as a semisimple algebra
exr-summary-and-transfer-c1.html:
Let n≥2 and let Cn⊆Mn(C) be the algebra of circulants of Chapter 11 Section 9.

  1. Explain why Cn acts semisimply on Cn, and write down its Wedderburn form as an abstract algebra.
  2. Prove that an X∈Mn(C) commutes with every circulant if and only if F∗XF is diagonal, and deduce Cn′=Cn.
  3. Verify @thm-double-commutant for A=Cn.

Hint for (b): first show that a matrix commuting with every diagonal matrix is diagonal, by testing against the matrix units Ekk.

exr-the-abelian-case-a1.title: A1
exr-the-abelian-case-a1.html:
1. Define the dual group G^ of a finite abelian group G, and say what its identity and inverses are.
  2. State why |G^|=|G|, naming the two results used.
  3. Write down the character matrix of G and state what its unitarity says about the characters.
  4. Determine whether the following are true, with a reason. (i) Every irreducible complex representation of a finite abelian group is one-dimensional. (ii) The book has proved G^≅G for every finite abelian G. (iii) The Fourier matrix of Chapter 11 Section 9 is the character matrix of Z/nZ. (iv) For A∈Cn and x∈Cn, Ax is the convolution of the first row of A with x.
  5. Explain in one sentence why the values of a character of a finite abelian group are roots of unity.

exr-the-abelian-case-b1.title: B1: The character table of the group of order three
exr-the-abelian-case-b1.title_html: B1: The character table of the group of order three
exr-the-abelian-case-b1.html:
Let G=Z/3Z and ω=e2πi/3.

  1. Write down the three characters and the character matrix.
  2. Verify one off-diagonal orthogonality relation by hand.
  3. Let a=2δ[0]−δ[1]−δ[2]∈C[G]. Compute Φ(a), write down the circulant Ψ(a), and state its eigenvalues.

exr-the-abelian-case-b2.title: B2: A product of two cyclic groups
exr-the-abelian-case-b2.title_html: B2: A product of two cyclic groups
exr-the-abelian-case-b2.html:
Let G=Z/2Z×Z/3Z and ω=e2πi/3.

  1. Use @thm-dual-group-iso (b) to list the six characters of G explicitly.
  2. Show that G is cyclic by exhibiting a generator, and say which character of G corresponds to which character of Z/6Z under your isomorphism.

exr-the-abelian-case-b3.title: B3: A transform and its inversion
exr-the-abelian-case-b3.title_html: B3: A transform and its inversion
exr-the-abelian-case-b3.html:
Let G=Z/4Z and let f be the function with values f([0]),f([1]),f([2]),f([3])=1,1,−1,−1.

  1. Compute f^(χj) for j=0,1,2,3.
  2. Recover f([1]) from @thm-fourier-inversion-on-a-group (b).
  3. Check Plancherel’s identity for f.

exr-the-abelian-case-c1.title: C1: The idempotents that do the splitting
exr-the-abelian-case-c1.title_html: C1: The idempotents that do the splitting
exr-the-abelian-case-c1.html:
Let G be a finite abelian group of order n. For χ∈G^ put εχ:=1n∑g∈Gχ(g)―δg∈C[G].

  1. Prove that Φ(εχ)(ψ) equals 1 when ψ=χ and 0 otherwise.
  2. Deduce that εχεψ=0 for χ≠ψ, that εχ2=εχ, and that ∑χεχ=δe.
  3. For G=Z/4Z write εχ1 out, and identify the matrix Ψ(εχ1) in terms of the Fourier vector f1 of Chapter 11 Section 9.

Hint for (a): the sum is an inner product of two characters.

exr-the-abelian-case-c2.title: C2: The double dual needs no choices
exr-the-abelian-case-c2.title_html: C2: The double dual needs no choices
exr-the-abelian-case-c2.html:
Let G be a finite abelian group. For g∈G define evg:G^→C× by evg(χ):=χ(g).

  1. Prove that evg∈G^^ and that g↦evg is a group homomorphism G→G^^.
  2. Prove that it is injective. Hint: the rows of the character matrix are indexed by the elements of G.
  3. Deduce that it is an isomorphism, and explain why this is not a second proof of @thm-dual-group-iso.

exr-the-abelian-case-c3.title: C3: The same theory over a finite field
exr-the-abelian-case-c3.title_html: C3: The same theory over a finite field
exr-the-abelian-case-c3.html:
Two properties of C were in use throughout this section: it contains n distinct n-th roots of unity, and n is invertible in it. They are not everything C contributed: algebraic closure was spent in @thm-abelian-characters-are-homomorphisms (a), and Section 8’s orthogonality relations were proved for complex representations only. But for one group and one field the conclusions can be checked directly with nothing more than those two properties. Take F=F5, G=Z/4Z and ω=2∈F5.

  1. Verify that ω has order 4 in F5×, and that 4 is invertible in F5.
  2. Write down the 4×4 matrix M with (M)mj=ωjm over F5 and check that 4−1∑mωjmω−km=δjk for j=1 and k=0,1.
  3. Let C be the circulant over F5 with first row (1,2,3,4). Compute M−1CM without inverting M, by evaluating the symbol at the powers of ω.

Hint for (c): the proof of @thm-circulant-diagonalization used only Sn=I and the geometric-series identity, both of which hold over F5.

exr-wedderburn-a1.title: A1
exr-wedderburn-a1.html:
1. State @thm-wedderburn with all of its hypotheses, and say which hypothesis fails for the upper triangular matrices in M2(C).
  2. Where in the proof is algebraic closure used, and what replaces the conclusion when it is dropped?
  3. A semisimple algebra over C has dimension 5. List all possibilities for its Wedderburn form.
  4. True or false, with a reason: a commutative semisimple algebra over C of dimension n is isomorphic to Cn.

exr-wedderburn-b1.title: B1: Determine which are semisimple
exr-wedderburn-b1.html:
Determine which of the following algebras over C are semisimple, and give the Wedderburn form of those that are. Justify your answer.

  1. The diagonal matrices in M3(C).
  2. C[x]/(x2).
  3. C[x]/(x2−1).

exr-wedderburn-b2.title: B2: A dimension count
exr-wedderburn-b2.html: Let A be a semisimple algebra over C with dim⁡A=8 and dim⁡Z(A)=5. Determine the Wedderburn form of A, and the dimensions of the irreducible A-spaces.

exr-wedderburn-b3.title: B3: The group algebra of a group of order three
exr-wedderburn-b3.title_html: B3: The group algebra of a group of order three
exr-wedderburn-b3.html: Let C3={1,g,g2} with g3=1. Imitating @exm-wedderburn-of-c4, produce an explicit algebra isomorphism C[C3]→C3 and write down the three idempotents.

exr-wedderburn-c1.title: C1: Simple plus semisimple
exr-wedderburn-c1.html:
Let F be algebraically closed and let A≠{0} be a finite-dimensional semisimple F-algebra.

  1. Prove that A is simple (has no two-sided ideal but {0} and A) if and only if k=1, that is, A≅Mn(F) for some n.
  2. Deduce that a finite-dimensional simple semisimple algebra over C has square dimension.

Hint for (a): in a product, the set of elements whose slots after the first are zero is a two-sided ideal.

exr-wedderburn-c2.title: C2: How often each irreducible appears
exr-wedderburn-c2.title_html: C2: How often each irreducible appears
exr-wedderburn-c2.html:
Keep the notation of @thm-wedderburn and of its proof, so that A=L1⊕⋯⊕Lm with each Lj isomorphic to exactly one Vi. Let mi be the number of indices j with Lj≅Vi. For A-spaces V,W write HomA(V,W) for the vector space of homomorphisms of A-spaces V→W.

  1. Prove that f↦f(1A) is a linear bijection HomA(A,V)→V for every A-space V, where A carries the regular representation.
  2. Prove that dim⁡HomA(Lj,Vi) is 1 if Lj≅Vi and 0 otherwise.
  3. Deduce that mi=ni: each irreducible appears in the regular representation exactly as many times as its dimension. Check the result against @cor-dimension-count.

Hint for (b): @thm-schurs-lemma, both parts.

exr-wedderburn-c3.title: C3: Change the field
exr-wedderburn-c3.html:
Let A={xI2+yQ:x,y∈R}⊆M2(R), where Q=(0−110).

  1. Prove that A is a semisimple R-algebra of dimension 2.
  2. Show that A is not isomorphic to a product Mn1(R)×⋯×Mnk(R), and identify which hypothesis of @thm-wedderburn fails.
  3. Prove that A is itself a division algebra over R and identify it.

lem-average-projection.title: The average of a representation is the projection onto the fixed space
lem-average-projection.title_html: The average of a representation is the projection onto the fixed space
lem-average-projection.html: Let ρ be a representation of a finite group G on a complex space V, and set VG:={v∈V:ρ(g)v=v for all g∈G},P:=1|G|∑g∈Gρ(g). Then VG is a subspace, P is a projection with imP=VG, and 1|G|∑g∈Gχρ(g)=dim⁡VG.

lem-element-has-finite-order.title: Order of an Element
lem-element-has-finite-order.html: Let G be a finite group and g∈G. Then there is a least integer m≥1 with gm=1, called the order of g. Moreover gk=gl if and only if m divides k−l, and ⟨g⟩:={gk:k∈Z}={1,g,g2,…,gm−1} is a subgroup of G with exactly m elements.

lem-family-and-generated-algebra.title: A Family and the Algebra It Generates
lem-family-and-generated-algebra.title_html: A Family and the Algebra It Generates
lem-family-and-generated-algebra.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F and let F⊆L(V) be any set of operators. Write A(F):=F⟨F⟩ for the subalgebra of L(V) generated by F (@def-generated-subalgebra). Then:

  1. A(F) contains F and idV, and is the span of idV together with all products S1S2⋯Sm with m≥1 and S1,…,Sm∈F;
  2. a subspace U⊆V is invariant under every member of F if and only if it is A(F)-invariant;
  3. an operator S∈L(V) commutes with every member of F if and only if it commutes with every element of A(F);
  4. if the members of F commute with one another, then A(F) is commutative.

lem-group-order-invertible.title: When the group order is invertible
lem-group-order-invertible.title_html: When the group order is invertible
lem-group-order-invertible.html: Let F be a field and m a positive integer. Then m⋅1F≠0 in F if and only if charF does not divide m.

lem-invariant-complement-heredity.title: Splitting Is Inherited by Invariant Subspaces
lem-invariant-complement-heredity.title_html: Splitting Is Inherited by Invariant Subspaces
lem-invariant-complement-heredity.html: Let A act semisimply on a finite-dimensional A-space V, and let W⊆V be A-invariant. Then W, with the action a↦ρ(a)|W, is an A-space, and A acts semisimply on W.

lem-matrix-units.title: The Matrix Unit Product Rule
lem-matrix-units.html: Let F be a field, n≥1, and 1≤i,j,k,l≤n. Then, in Mn(F), EijEkl=δjkEil,andEijXEkl=xjkEil  for every X=(xpq). Moreover E11+E22+⋯+Enn=In.

lem-nilpotent-ideal-acts-as-zero.title: A Nilpotent Ideal Is Invisible
lem-nilpotent-ideal-acts-as-zero.html: Let A be an F-algebra and let I⊆A be a two-sided ideal which is nilpotent: for some m≥1, every product a1a2⋯am of m elements of I is 0. Then I⊆radA.

lem-one-vector-density.title: Matching on One Vector
lem-one-vector-density.html: Let W be a finite-dimensional vector space over F and let B⊆End(W) be a subalgebra with idW∈B which acts semisimply on W: every B-invariant subspace of W has a B-invariant complement (@def-semisimple-algebra). Then for every t∈B″ and every w∈W there is b∈B with bw=tw.

lem-orbit-of-a-vector.title: An Irreducible Algebra Moves One Vector Everywhere
lem-orbit-of-a-vector.title_html: An Irreducible Algebra Moves One Vector Everywhere
lem-orbit-of-a-vector.html: Let A⊆End(V) be a subalgebra with idV∈A, acting irreducibly on V. Then Av:={av:a∈A}=V for every v≠0.

lem-trace-of-sandwich.title: The trace of a two-sided multiplication
lem-trace-of-sandwich.title_html: The trace of a two-sided multiplication
lem-trace-of-sandwich.html: Let V and W be finite-dimensional vector spaces over a field F, let A∈L(V) and B∈L(W), and let Φ:L(V,W)→L(V,W),Φ(f)=B∘f∘A. Then Φ is linear and trΦ=(trA)(trB).

prp-adjoint-closed-acts-semisimply.title: Closed Under Adjoints Implies Semisimple
prp-adjoint-closed-acts-semisimply.html:
Let V be a finite-dimensional inner product space over F=R or F=C, and let A⊆L(V) be a subalgebra containing idV and closed under adjoints: T∈A implies T∗∈A (@def-adjoint). Then:

  1. for every A-invariant subspace U, the orthogonal complement U⊥ is A-invariant, and V=U⊕U⊥; in particular A acts semisimply on V;
  2. V is a direct sum of pairwise orthogonal irreducible A-invariant subspaces.

prp-center-of-matrix-algebra.title: The Center of the Matrix Algebra Is the Scalars
prp-center-of-matrix-algebra.title_html: The Center of the Matrix Algebra Is the Scalars
prp-center-of-matrix-algebra.html: Let F be any field and n≥1. Then Z(Mn(F))=FIn. Equivalently, for a finite-dimensional V≠{0}, the operators commuting with every operator on V are exactly the scalar multiples of idV.

prp-character-basic.title: Basic properties of characters
prp-character-basic.html:
Let ρ be a representation of a finite group G on a complex space V, with character χ=χρ. Then:

  1. χ(1)=dim⁡V;
  2. χ is a class function: χ(xgx−1)=χ(g) for all g,x∈G;
  3. equivalent representations have equal characters;
  4. if V=U⊕W with both summands G-invariant, then χ=χρ|U+χρ|W;
  5. χ(g−1)=χ(g)― for every g∈G, and |χ(g)|≤χ(1).

prp-commutant-is-algebra.title: Properties of the Commutant
prp-commutant-is-algebra.html:
Let A be an algebra over F and S,T⊆A.

  1. S′ is a subalgebra of A; in particular Z(A) is a commutative subalgebra.
  2. If S⊆T, then T′⊆S′.
  3. S⊆S″.
  4. S′=S‴.

prp-dimension-class-functions.title: The class functions have dimension the number of classes
prp-dimension-class-functions.title_html: The class functions have dimension the number of classes
prp-dimension-class-functions.html: Let G be a finite group with conjugacy classes C1,…,Ck. For each j let 1Cj:G→C be the function that is 1 on Cj and 0 elsewhere. Then (1C1,…,1Ck) is a basis of Cl(G), and dim⁡Cl(G)=k.

prp-dual-group-is-a-group.title: The Dual Group Is a Group
prp-dual-group-is-a-group.title_html: The Dual Group Is a Group
prp-dual-group-is-a-group.html: For a finite abelian group G, the set G^ with the pointwise operation is a finite abelian group. Its identity is the trivial character χ0, with χ0(g)=1 for every g, and the inverse of χ is χ―, the function g↦χ(g)―.

prp-dual-group-order.title: The Dual Group Has the Same Size
prp-dual-group-order.title_html: The Dual Group Has the Same Size
prp-dual-group-order.html: For every finite abelian group G, |G^|=|G|.

prp-generated-is-span-of-words.title: What the Generated Subalgebra Contains
prp-generated-is-span-of-words.html: Let A be an algebra over F and S⊆A. Then F⟨S⟩ is the span of 1A together with all finite products s1s2⋯sk with k≥1 and s1,…,sk∈S.

prp-hom-representation.title: The representation on the space of linear maps
prp-hom-representation.title_html: The representation on the space of linear maps
prp-hom-representation.html: Let ρ,σ be representations of a finite group G on complex spaces V,W. Then π above is a representation of G on L(V,W), its character is χπ(g)=χσ(g)χρ(g)―, and its fixed space is the space LG(V,W):={f∈L(V,W):fρ(g)=σ(g)f for all g∈G} of maps intertwining ρ and σ (@def-equivalent-representations); for W=V and σ=ρ this is the commutant EndC[G](V) of @def-intertwining-map. Consequently 1|G|∑g∈Gχσ(g)χρ(g)―=dim⁡LG(V,W).{#eq-intertwiner-count}

prp-left-ideals-of-matrix-algebra.title: The Left Ideals of M_n(F)
prp-left-ideals-of-matrix-algebra.title_html: The Left Ideals of Mn(F)
prp-left-ideals-of-matrix-algebra.html:
Let F be a field and n≥1. For a subspace W⊆M1×n(F) of row vectors, put LW:={X∈Mn(F):row(X)⊆W}.

  1. LW is a left ideal of Mn(F), and dim⁡LW=ndim⁡W.
  2. Every left ideal L of Mn(F) equals LW for exactly one W, namely the span of the union of the row spaces of the elements of L: W=span(⋃X∈Lrow(X)).
  3. W↦LW is an inclusion-preserving bijection from subspaces of M1×n(F) onto left ideals of Mn(F). The minimal non-zero left ideals are the LW with dim⁡W=1.
  4. Taking W=span(ej⊤) gives the column ideal Cj of @exm-first-ideals (c), of dimension n, and Mn(F)=C1⊕⋯⊕Cn as a direct sum of left ideals.

prp-map-out-of-simple-is-injective.title: Maps Out of a Simple Algebra
prp-map-out-of-simple-is-injective.title_html: Maps Out of a Simple Algebra
prp-map-out-of-simple-is-injective.html: Let A be a simple F-algebra, let B≠{0} be an F-algebra, and let φ:A→B be an algebra homomorphism (@def-algebra-homomorphism). Then φ is injective.

prp-polynomial-algebra-dimension.title: The Algebra Generated by One Operator
prp-polynomial-algebra-dimension.title_html: The Algebra Generated by One Operator
prp-polynomial-algebra-dimension.html: Let V≠{0} be finite-dimensional over F and let T∈L(V) have minimal polynomial mT, of degree d. Then F[T]:={p(T):p∈F[x]} is a commutative subalgebra of L(V), it equals F⟨{T}⟩, and (idV,T,T2,…,Td−1) is a basis of it. In particular dim⁡F[T]=deg⁡mT.

prp-semisimple-algebra-all-reps-semisimp.title: A Semisimple Algebra Has No Other Kind of Representation
prp-semisimple-algebra-all-reps-semisimp.title_html: A Semisimple Algebra Has No Other Kind of Representation
prp-semisimple-algebra-all-reps-semisimp.html: Let A be a semisimple F-algebra and let V be any finite-dimensional A-space. Then A acts semisimply on V.

prp-semisimple-has-zero-radical.title: A Semisimple Algebra Has Zero Radical
prp-semisimple-has-zero-radical.title_html: A Semisimple Algebra Has Zero Radical
prp-semisimple-has-zero-radical.html: Let A be a semisimple F-algebra. Then radA={0}.

thm-abelian-characters-are-homomorphisms.title: Characters of an Abelian Group Are Homomorphisms
thm-abelian-characters-are-homomorphisms.title_html: Characters of an Abelian Group Are Homomorphisms
thm-abelian-characters-are-homomorphisms.html:
Let G be a finite abelian group and let the field be C. Then:

  1. every irreducible representation of G is one-dimensional;
  2. a one-dimensional representation of G is the same thing as a group homomorphism χ:G→C×, and the character of that representation is χ itself;
  3. every one-dimensional representation is irreducible, and two of them are equivalent if and only if they are equal;
  4. for every such χ and every g∈G, the number χ(g) is an m-th root of unity, where m is the order of g (@lem-element-has-finite-order); in particular |χ(g)|=1 and χ(g)−1=χ(g)―=χ(g−1).

thm-algebra-first-isomorphism.title: First Isomorphism Theorem for Algebras
thm-algebra-first-isomorphism.html: Let φ:A→B be a homomorphism of F-algebras. Then kerφ is a two-sided ideal of A, imφ is a subalgebra of B, and the rule φ¯:A/kerφ→B,φ¯(x+kerφ)=φ(x), defines an injective algebra homomorphism with image imφ. Hence A/kerφ≅imφ as F-algebras.

thm-burnside.title: Burnside’s Theorem
thm-burnside.html: Let F be an algebraically closed field, that is, one in which every non-constant polynomial in F[x] has a root. Let V be a vector space over F with 1≤dim⁡V<∞, and let A⊆End(V) be a subalgebra with idV∈A. If V is irreducible as an A-space, then A=End(V).

thm-cayley-for-algebras.title: Left Multiplication Embeds an Algebra in Its Own Operators
thm-cayley-for-algebras.title_html: Left Multiplication Embeds an Algebra in Its Own Operators
thm-cayley-for-algebras.html: Let A be an algebra over F. For a∈A define La:A→A by La(x)=ax. Then L:A→L(A),a↦La, is an injective algebra homomorphism. If dimF⁡A=n<∞, then A is isomorphic to a subalgebra of Mn(F).

thm-character-matrix-is-fourier-matrix.title: The Character Matrix Is the Fourier Matrix
thm-character-matrix-is-fourier-matrix.title_html: The Character Matrix Is the Fourier Matrix
thm-character-matrix-is-fourier-matrix.html: For G=Z/nZ with the orderings above, the character matrix of @def-character-matrix is exactly the Fourier matrix F of @thm-fourier-matrix-unitary: (U)mj=ωjmn=(F)mj(0≤m,j≤n−1). In particular the unitarity of F and the orthonormality of the characters of Z/nZ are the same statement.

thm-character-orthogonality.title: Orthogonality of Irreducible Characters
thm-character-orthogonality.html: Let G be a finite group and let ρ on V and σ on W be irreducible complex representations of G. Then ⟨χσ,χρ⟩={1,if ρ≅σ,0,if ρ≇σ. In particular the characters of pairwise inequivalent irreducible complex representations form an orthonormal list in Cl(G).

thm-characters-span-class-functions.title: The Irreducible Characters Are a Basis of the Class Functions
thm-characters-span-class-functions.title_html: The Irreducible Characters Are a Basis of the Class Functions
thm-characters-span-class-functions.html: Let G be a finite group with k conjugacy classes. Then G has exactly k irreducible complex representations up to equivalence, and their characters χ1,…,χk form an orthonormal basis of Cl(G).

thm-circulants-are-the-group-algebra.title: Circulants Are the Group Algebra of the Cyclic Group
thm-circulants-are-the-group-algebra.title_html: Circulants Are the Group Algebra of the Cyclic Group
thm-circulants-are-the-group-algebra.html:
Let n≥1 and let Cn⊆Mn(C) be the algebra of circulants (@cor-circulants-algebra). Let Ψ:C[Z/nZ]→Mn(C) be the linear map with Ψ(δ[m]):=Sm(m=0,1,…,n−1), where S is the cyclic shift. Then:

  1. Ψ is an isomorphism of algebras onto Cn, and Ψ(∑mcmδ[m]) is the circulant C with first row c;
  2. Ψ(a) is the matrix of the map “multiply by a” on C[Z/nZ], in the ordered basis B=(δ[0], δ[−1], δ[−2], …, δ[−(n−1)]);
  3. F∗Ψ(a)F is the diagonal matrix whose j-th entry is Φ(a)(χj); that is, Φ is Ψ followed by conjugating with F and reading off the diagonal.

thm-double-commutant.title: Double Commutant Theorem
thm-double-commutant.html: Let F be any field, let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over F, and let A⊆End(V) be a subalgebra with idV∈A. Assume that A acts semisimply on V: every A-invariant subspace of V has an A-invariant complement (@def-semisimple-algebra). Then A″=A.

thm-dual-group-iso.title: The Dual of a Product of Cyclic Groups
thm-dual-group-iso.title_html: The Dual of a Product of Cyclic Groups
thm-dual-group-iso.html:
Let G and H be finite abelian groups. Then:

  1. if G is cyclic, then G^≅G;
  2. G×H^≅G^×H^;
  3. consequently, if G is a direct product of finitely many finite cyclic groups, then G^≅G.

thm-fourier-inversion-on-a-group.title: Fourier Inversion on a Finite Abelian Group
thm-fourier-inversion-on-a-group.title_html: Fourier Inversion on a Finite Abelian Group
thm-fourier-inversion-on-a-group.html:
Let G be a finite abelian group of order n, with orderings fixed as in @def-character-matrix and character matrix U. Then:

  1. U is unitary, and the n functions n−1/2χj form an orthonormal basis of the space CG of all functions G→C;
  2. (Inversion) every f:G→C satisfies f(g)=1n∑χ∈G^f^(χ)χ(g)―(g∈G);
  3. (Plancherel) ∑g∈G|f(g)|2=1n∑χ∈G^|f^(χ)|2.

thm-group-algebra-splits.title: The Group Algebra of an Abelian Group Splits
thm-group-algebra-splits.title_html: The Group Algebra of an Abelian Group Splits
thm-group-algebra-splits.html: Let G be a finite abelian group of order n, and let CG^ denote the algebra of all functions G^→C with pointwise operations, which is a product of n copies of C. Then Φ:C[G]→CG^,Φ(∑gcgδg)(χ):=∑gcgχ(g), is an isomorphism of algebras. For G=Z/nZ it is the discrete Fourier transform c↦c^=nFc of Chapter 11 Section 9, and its multiplicativity is @thm-convolution-theorem (b).

thm-maschke.title: Maschke’s Theorem
thm-maschke.html: Let G be a finite group and F a field whose characteristic does not divide |G|. Let ρ be a representation of G on a finite-dimensional space V over F, and let U⊆V be a G-invariant subspace. Then there is a G-invariant subspace W⊆V with V=U⊕W.

thm-matrix-algebra-is-simple.title: The Matrix Algebra Has No Proper Two-Sided Ideals
thm-matrix-algebra-is-simple.title_html: The Matrix Algebra Has No Proper Two-Sided Ideals
thm-matrix-algebra-is-simple.html: Let F be any field and n≥1. The only two-sided ideals of Mn(F) are {0} and Mn(F). Consequently, for a finite-dimensional vector space V≠{0} over F, the only two-sided ideals of L(V) are {0} and L(V).

thm-representations-are-modules-over-the.title: Representations of G are representations of F[G]
thm-representations-are-modules-over-the.title_html: Representations of G are representations of F[G]
thm-representations-are-modules-over-the.html: Let G be a finite group, F a field and V a finite-dimensional vector space over F. The assignment ρ ⟼ ρ~,ρ~(∑g∈Gagδg):=∑g∈Gagρ(g), is a bijection from the set of representations ρ:G→GL(V) onto the set of algebra homomorphisms F[G]→End(V) (@def-algebra-homomorphism) — that is, onto the ways of making V an F[G]-space in the sense of @def-representation-of-an-algebra. Moreover a subspace U⊆V is G-invariant for ρ if and only if ρ~(a)U⊆U for every a∈F[G].

thm-schurs-lemma.title: Schur’s Lemma
thm-schurs-lemma.html:
Let A be an F-algebra.

  1. Let V and W be irreducible A-spaces and let φ:V→W be an A-map. Then either φ=0 or φ is an isomorphism of A-spaces. No hypothesis on F is needed.
  2. Suppose in addition that F is algebraically closed, and let V be an irreducible A-space. Then every A-map φ:V→V is a scalar: φ=λidV for some λ∈F. Equivalently, EndA(V)={λidV:λ∈F}.

thm-semisimple-iff-sum-of-simples.title: Complete Reducibility
thm-semisimple-iff-sum-of-simples.html:
Let A be an F-algebra and let V be a finite-dimensional A-space. The following are equivalent:

  1. A acts semisimply on V;
  2. V is a sum of irreducible A-invariant subspaces;
  3. V is a direct sum of finitely many irreducible A-invariant subspaces.

Here a sum over the empty family is {0}, so all three hold when V={0}. No hypothesis is placed on F.

thm-semisimple-operator-iff-semisimple-a.title: The Two Meanings of Semisimple Agree
thm-semisimple-operator-iff-semisimple-a.title_html: The Two Meanings of Semisimple Agree
thm-semisimple-operator-iff-semisimple-a.html:
Let V≠{0} be a finite-dimensional vector space over F and let T∈L(V). The following are equivalent:

  1. T is semisimple in the sense of @def-semisimple-operator, that is, mT is a product of distinct monic irreducible polynomials;
  2. F[T] acts semisimply on V: every T-invariant subspace has a T-invariant complement;
  3. V is a sum of irreducible F[T]-invariant subspaces.

No hypothesis is placed on F.

thm-wedderburn.title: Wedderburn’s Structure Theorem, Algebraically Closed Case
thm-wedderburn.title_html: Wedderburn’s Structure Theorem, Algebraically Closed Case
thm-wedderburn.html: Let F be an algebraically closed field and let A≠{0} be a semisimple finite-dimensional F-algebra: every left ideal of A has a complementary left ideal. Then there are an integer k≥1, integers n1,…,nk≥1 and an isomorphism of F-algebras A≅Mn1(F)×⋯×Mnk(F). Moreover k and the multiset {n1,…,nk} depend only on A: they are the number of isomorphism classes of irreducible A-spaces and their dimensions.
